facts.fact: ITWeb Africa reports that Nigeria is preparing a law to regulate AI through the National Digital Economy and E-Governance Bill, expected to be approved by the end of March, with a risk-based framework, annual impact assessments for high-risk AI systems and fines of up to 10 million naira or 2% of an AI provider's Nigerian revenue; the document gives no event date, so its published date is used.

facts.fact: TechCabal reports that Nigeria has a proposed Artificial Intelligence Bill with a risk-based model, a licensing regime for building or deploying certain AI systems and an AI Council, and that it was under debate; the document gives no event date, so its published date is used.

Okolo and Raji state that four consolidated AI bills passed second reading in Nigeria's House of Representatives on 3 December 2024, among them the Control of Usage of Artificial Intelligence Technology in Nigeria Bill, 2023 (HB.942), which provides for ethical principles, risk assessment, data governance, safety and security, and penalties.

facts.fact: The Liberalist states that the Nigeria Data Protection Commission issued the General Application and Implementation Directive in 2025, whose Article 43 names artificial intelligence and requires controllers deploying it to document parameters, assess disparate outcomes and test the system, and whose Article 44 tells them to cease using AI systems that pose undue risks to human rights; it calls these current regulatory text.

note: The Nigeria Data Protection Act s.37 rule on automated decisions is a data protection rule and gives no fact; the document says a dedicated AI law is being developed, which is an intention with no draft named.

facts.fact: TechTrends Africa reports that as of 2025 Nigeria was still working through the National Artificial Intelligence Commission (Establishment) Bill, which would create a commission with regulatory authority, and that it had not cleared the National Assembly (article published 2026-07-28; the date of the status is given only as 2025).
